summary:
Charter covers a new McKinsey Global Institute report arguing the AI jobs outlook is less dire than headlines suggest: over the next decade the US economy could create more jobs than automation eliminates, new roles could pay better than displaced ones, and in understaffed fields such as nursing AI could relieve overwork.

The complication is occupational mobility rather than job scarcity. MGI estimates roughly 11 million US workers, about 7% of the current workforce, may need to move into entirely different occupations by 2035, and only about one in seven workers has a clear pathway into such a transition.

McKinsey senior partner and MGI director Tanguy Catlin told Charter the scale and duration of the shift is unprecedented. Around 770,000 workers may need to switch occupational groups each year, roughly 3.6 times the historical average. Catlin compares the required job migration to what the US experienced during covid, but notes the pandemic disruption lasted two years while this transition is expected to last a decade.

The piece is macro labor market commentary on AI, reskilling and career pathways. It does not address workplace operations topics such as visitor management, desk or room booking, hybrid and return to office policy, attendance tracking, facilities management, or workplace analytics tooling.
